LinkedInB2B brands, hiring, thought leadershipShort posts with a clear point, documents, expert views, company news
InstagramConsumer brands, visual products, local businessesPhotos, short video (Reels), Stories, behind-the-scenes
FacebookLocal business, communities, events, older audiencesGroups, events, customer questions, local news
TikTokShort video, younger audiences, product discoveryQuick tips, demos, trends that fit your brand
YouTubeHow-to content, product demos, long-term search trafficTutorials, explainers, customer stories
X (Twitter)News, support, quick updatesShort updates, replies, live events
PinterestHome, food, fashion, design, planningTall images that link to useful pages

This table is a starting point, not a rule. Check where your own customers spend time. Ask new customers how they found you. The answer often points to the right platform faster than any chart.

How to start with social media management: 8 steps

Use this process whether you run one account or ten.

Step 1: Set one or two goals

Pick goals that tie to the business. Examples: more enquiries from LinkedIn, faster replies to customers, or more visits to your product pages. Avoid "get more followers" as the only goal. Followers do not pay your bills.

Step 2: Know your audience

Write down who you want to reach: their job or situation, the questions they ask and where they spend time online. Use your customer emails, sales calls and search data. Ten real questions from customers are worth more than a guess.

Step 3: Choose your platforms

You do not need every platform. Choose the two or three where your audience is active and where you can post well. A business that sells to other businesses often starts with LinkedIn and YouTube. A shop that sells to consumers may start with Instagram and TikTok.

Step 4: Set up your profiles

Use the same name, logo and short description on every platform. Add a link to your site. Write a bio that says who you help and what you do. Make sure each profile is complete before you post.

Step 5: Plan your content

Choose three to five topics your audience cares about. These are your content pillars. Then fill a content calendar with posts for each pillar. A mix works well: some posts that teach, some that show your work, some that start a conversation, and a few that ask for action.

Step 6: Create and schedule

Write posts in batches, once a week or once a month. Then schedule them in a tool. Batching saves time and keeps your voice steady. Leave room in the calendar for news and timely posts.

Step 7: Engage every day

Scheduling is not enough. Set aside time each day to reply to comments and messages, and to comment on other people's posts. Social platforms are built for conversation, and accounts that only broadcast get less back.

Step 8: Measure and improve

Once a month, look at what worked. Keep the topics and formats that earned replies, clicks and enquiries. Drop the ones that did not. Then update the calendar for next month.

A worked example: a small B2B software company

This example is illustrative. It shows how the steps fit together. The numbers are a sample plan, not results.

A company sells scheduling software to dental clinics. It has one marketer and two hours a day for social media.

StepWhat the company decides
GoalBook 10 demo calls a month from social media
AudienceClinic owners and practice managers
PlatformsLinkedIn first, YouTube for short how-to videos
Content pillarsFewer missed appointments; running a clinic; product tips; customer stories
RhythmThree LinkedIn posts a week, one video every two weeks
Daily task20 minutes replying to comments and messages
Monthly reviewCount demo calls, replies and clicks per post type

After two months, the marketer sees that posts about missed appointments get the most replies and the most clicks. The plan shifts: more of those posts, fewer general tips. That is the loop in action: plan, post, measure, change.

What goes in a content calendar?

A content calendar is a plan of what you will post, where and when. It does not need to be fancy. A spreadsheet works. Each row needs:

  • The date and time
  • The platform
  • The content pillar
  • The text and the image or video
  • The link, if there is one
  • The owner and the approval status

Plan two to four weeks ahead. Keep a short list of spare ideas in case you need a post fast.

How do you manage a community?

Community management is the part of the job where you talk with people. It builds trust faster than posting does.

  • Reply fast. Set a target, such as the same business day. Tell customers your hours on your profile.
  • Be human. Use plain words. Use the person's name. Skip stock phrases.
  • Answer in public, then move private. Give a short answer in the comments. Take account details to direct messages or email.
  • Thank people. A short thanks for a share, a review or a good question costs little.
  • Know when to hand off. Write a short guide: which questions go to sales, which go to support and who handles complaints.

An example reply to a complaint, with the aim of fixing it and showing others you care: "Hi Sam, sorry the order arrived late. We have sent you a direct message to find out what happened and make it right." It is short, it names the person and it moves the details out of the public thread.

What is social listening, and why do it?

Social listening means tracking mentions of your brand, products, rivals and topics across social media, including posts that do not tag you. You then act on what you find.

Use it to:

  • Find customers who ask a question you can answer
  • Spot a problem early, before it grows
  • See what people say about rivals, and which gaps they point out
  • Collect ideas for content from the real words customers use

You can start for free. Set up saved searches on each platform for your brand name, common misspellings and two or three key topics. Check them each morning. Paid tools collect these searches in one place and add reports.

How should you handle a social media crisis?

A crisis is a fast-growing wave of negative attention, such as a product fault, a bad ad or a staff error. Plan before it happens. A short plan has five points:

  1. Pause scheduled posts. A cheerful promo during a crisis makes it worse.
  2. Find the facts. Talk to the people involved before you reply in public.
  3. Reply once, clearly. Say what happened, what you are doing and when you will update. Do not argue.
  4. Move details private. Offer direct contact to people who were harmed.
  5. Review afterwards. Write down what went wrong and change your process.

Name one person with the authority to approve a reply. Slow approvals are a common cause of bad crisis handling.

What skills does a social media manager need?

If you are hiring, or choosing an agency, look for these skills:

  • Writing. Clear, short text that sounds like your brand.
  • Basic design and video. Enough to make clean images and short clips, or to brief a designer.
  • Analytics. Reading reports and drawing a simple conclusion.
  • Customer care. Staying calm and polite with upset people.
  • Planning. Keeping a calendar and meeting deadlines.
  • Platform knowledge. Knowing how each platform shows posts and what its rules are.
  • Judgment. Knowing what not to post.

Ask for samples of real work, and ask what they measured and what they changed because of it.

A second example: a local service business

This example is also illustrative. A plumbing company has one office manager who handles social media for 30 minutes a day.

StepWhat the company decides
GoalMore calls from homeowners in its service area
PlatformsFacebook (local groups and page) and a Google Business Profile
Content pillarsSimple home fixes; before and after jobs; seasonal checks; meet the team
RhythmTwo posts a week and a photo after each finished job, with the customer's permission
Daily taskReply to every comment and message the same day
Monthly reviewCount calls and messages that mention Facebook, and which posts led to them

The company asks each new caller, "How did you find us?" and records the answer. After a quarter, it sees which posts brought calls and repeats those. It needs no expensive tool, just a steady routine and one number to track.

Which social media management tools do you need?

A social media management tool brings scheduling, replies, monitoring and reporting into one place. Many tools exist. Most cover these jobs:

JobWhat the tool does
Scheduling and calendarLets you plan and publish posts to several accounts from one screen
InboxGathers comments and messages from all platforms in one list
ListeningFinds mentions of your brand and topics, even when you are not tagged
AnalyticsShows reach, engagement, clicks and growth over time
Team workflowLets several people draft, review and approve posts

Choose by need, not by feature count. A solo founder needs scheduling and a simple report. A team of five needs approvals and a shared inbox. Try a free plan or trial before you pay. Also check which platforms the tool supports, because not all support every one.

What should you measure?

Pick numbers that match your goals. Start with a short list.

  • Reach and impressions: how many people saw your posts.
  • Engagement: likes, comments, shares and saves.
  • Click-throughs: visits from a post to your site.
  • Response time: how fast you reply to messages.
  • Leads and sales: enquiries and orders that started on social media. Track these with tagged links and your analytics tool.

Reach shows that people saw you. Leads and sales show that it paid off. Report both, and say which one your goal depends on.

Where do paid social and influencers fit?

Organic posts reach the people who already follow you. Paid social ads reach new people, and you choose the audience. Most teams start with organic work, learn what gets a response, and then put a small budget behind the best posts.

Influencer work means paying or partnering with people who already have an audience. Pick people whose followers match your buyers, not only the biggest numbers. Agree the deliverables, the dates and the disclosure rules in writing, because many countries require posts to say when they are sponsored.

Both belong in the plan, but they should not replace daily management. Ads send people to an account. The account still has to look active, answer questions and give a reason to follow.

How do you set up a team workflow?

Once more than one person posts, you need a simple workflow so mistakes do not reach the public. A basic version has four stages:

  1. Draft. The writer prepares the post and the image.
  2. Review. A second person checks facts, spelling and tone.
  3. Approve. The owner signs off, and a lawyer or compliance lead if your industry needs one.
  4. Schedule. The post goes into the calendar with a date, a time and a link tagged for tracking.

Write down your brand voice in one page: how you sound, words you use, words you avoid and how you handle humor. A shared voice guide keeps posts consistent when several people write them, and it makes handover easier when someone leaves.

What does a good monthly report look like?

A report is only useful if it leads to a decision. Keep it to one page. Include:

  1. Goal and result. What you aimed for and what happened.
  2. Top three posts. What they had in common.
  3. Bottom three posts. What to stop doing.
  4. What customers said. Common questions and complaints.
  5. Next month's changes. Two or three actions, with owners.

Compare each month with the one before. Do not compare your small account with a large brand. The point is to see whether your own work is improving.

How much do social media management services cost?

There is no standard price. It depends on how many platforms you use, how often you post, how much video you need, whether ads are included and who does the work. Agencies, freelancers and tools all price differently, and published prices change often, so ask for current quotes.

The cost has three parts:

  • People. Your own staff time, or a freelancer or agency fee.
  • Tools. Scheduling, design and reporting software, often paid by month.
  • Ad spend. The money you pay to platforms if you run paid posts. This is separate from management.

To compare options, add staff hours to tool cost. A simple, illustrative check: if you spend 10 hours a week on social media and your time is worth a set hourly rate, multiply the two and compare the result with an agency quote. Do not forget that the cheaper option may lack video or reporting.

In-house, freelancer or agency?

OptionGood forWatch out for
In-houseTeams that know the product well and want controlOne person cannot cover design, video, replies and reports
FreelancerSmall budgets and one or two platformsCover during holidays or illness
AgencySeveral platforms, video and reporting at onceDistance from your product, so give them access to experts

Many companies mix the options. They keep strategy and replies in-house and outsource design or video.

When you talk to an agency, ask for a written scope, who will write your posts, how often you will get reports and what is in them, how they handle a negative comment, and how you can leave the contract.

How is AI changing social media management?

AI tools can now suggest post ideas, draft captions, resize images and sort replies. They save time on first drafts and repeat tasks.

Use them with care. Always read and edit what an AI tool writes. Check facts, keep your own voice, and do not let a tool reply to a customer in your name without review. A fast wrong answer does more harm than a slow right one.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Being on every platform. Do fewer well.
  • Posting only sales messages. Mix in useful and human posts.
  • Ignoring replies. Social media is a two-way channel.
  • Skipping the plan. Posting when you remember leads to gaps.
  • Counting only followers. Track enquiries and sales.
  • Using one post for every platform. Each platform has its own format and tone.
  • Not saying who is in charge. Name one owner for each account.

A quick checklist

  • One or two clear goals
  • A named audience
  • Two or three platforms
  • Complete profiles with the same branding
  • Three to five content pillars
  • A content calendar for the next two to four weeks
  • A daily time block for replies
  • A monthly report with decisions

Final thoughts

Social media management works best when it is steady, simple and tied to a goal. Start with one plan, run it for a month and review what happened. If you also want your social work to support search and AI search visibility, Reinforce Lab can help with a free diagnostic.

Do you know about Anchor text optimization in SEO?

You must be thinking about how this thing can be optimized as well?

The answer is obvious!

So if you want to know “what is anchor text optimization,” you are in the right place!

When you optimize your content, you have to optimize all little things.

Every anchor text has an impact, so a relevant anchor text helps to get rank and improves your authority.

But do you know anchor text can be the reason for the getting penalty as well?

Yes, optimizing anchor text is crucial, and you must know how to do it properly.

This blog will discuss the anchor text optimization process step by step and guide you to avoid the google penguin penalty.

So let’s start with:

What is Anchor Text Optimization

 

The visible and clickable text that we see as part of a hyperlink from one website to another is anchor text (or link text).

SEO experts consider it one of the most significant parts of on-page and off-page optimization as a general principle of SEO.

There are multiple sides to this issue, as there are to most elements of SEO.

Search engines like Google use anchor text to gauge the relevance and value of a webpage.

A distinct color or an underline usually differentiates the anchor text.

From one of our blog posts, here’s an example of the anchor text “content writing service”:

 

The following is how the exact anchor text appears in HTML code (the anchor text is bolded):

 

As now you know what an anchor text is, let’s get to know about:

Different Types of Anchor Text

Here I will mention 10 types of anchor text that are widely used for the optimization:

Exact Match Anchor Text 

 

The term “exact match anchor text” refers to employing the page’s targeted keyword as anchor text.

For Example, the anchor text for this page is “anchor text.”

 

Partial Match Anchor Text

 

When using partial match anchor text, you combine your target term with other keywords.

For Example, when optimizing for “SEO audit,” you can use “understanding SEO Audit” as the anchor text.

 

Phrase Match Anchor Text

 

The phrase you intend to rank for is combined with other keywords in this type of anchor text.

“How to Use Anchor Text for SEO” is an example.

 

Branded Anchor Text

 

Branded anchor text is one of the most used and effective things to optimize.

This sort of anchored text includes your company’s name, ” Reinforce lab,” for Example.

 

Naked Anchor Text

 

The URL is given as the anchor text in naked anchor text.

For Example, the anchor text can be reinforcelabdevelopment.kinsta.cloud.  

Because it can look odd in the middle of a paragraph, this is a less popular approach to using text.

 

Generic Anchor Text

 

A call to action is essentially a generic anchor text (CTA).

“Learn more” or “get a quote” are two examples.

 

Long Tail Anchor Text

 

Long-tail anchors are like half anchors but longer.

You may add your keyword along with descriptive, generic, or branded keywords.

Long-tail anchors might incorporate subheadings or headlines.

 

Related Anchor Text

 

This particular kind of anchor text links to a page by using a variant of the target term.

Keyword variation can be an excellent choice to work with this type of anchor text.

 

Random Anchor Text 

 

Certain link analysis technologies can group random and generic anchors into the same group.

While they are not as general as “click here,” random anchor words might contain phrases that are not directly connected to the target keyword.

An excellent example of an anchor is an in-depth article.

 

Image Anchor

 

CTAs are similar to picture anchor text. In this scenario, you’ll use anchor text on an image.”

The anchor text would be “night view Today!” as a button on an image.

For your photographs, you’ll also need to supply alt text.

 

So the wait is over and without any further delay, let’s dive into our main topic, which is:

Anchor text Optimization in SEO: How to do it?

 

1. Avoid Keyword Stuffing

 

The truth is that you would not want a lot of inbound links coming to your site for two reasons:

1) It does not look natural, and

2) You only want high-quality links connecting to your site.

Though it is always an intelligent option to optimize your anchor text.

You usually only need to do so for approximately 10% to 20% of your links and make sure they are the best.

This is sufficient to inform Google of the terms you wish to rank for.

Remember that 10 authoritative, well-respected links are worth more than 30 low-quality connections.

 

2. Variation is Helpful

 

Your distinctive and diversified approach is preferable when building an anchor text strategy that aids SEO.

This goes against the grain of most SEO advice, which emphasizes the need to use anchor texts in specific ratios.

The ideal way to optimize a home page is to utilize 5% exact match, 20% phrase match, and 10% key phrases.

In most circumstances, your advice depends on who gives it and what sector you work in.

Anchor text practices can usually be established by following the instructions provided and making little adjustments here and there.

A more in-depth review is needed to determine what works best for your SEO and organic results once you’ve established a baseline.

If you’re having trouble, you can always check out what your competitors are doing!

Recommendation: Based on research showing the impact of Penguin 4.0 on a wide range of companies in various areas.

 

3. Provide Relevant Resources, Not Random

 

Search engines have detected additional ranking signals throughout time.

Link relevance, or how closely a page’s topic is related to another’s, stands out.

Page A and page B search rankings may benefit from a related link.

“Link relevance” occurs when people link to other websites because of:

  1. Page topic
  2. Anchor text on the page

Relevance signals are more substantial when a link refers to relevant content than unrelated content.

A link to a coffee shop’s website from a page on the best New York City coffee is more likely to send a relevant signal to Google than a link to a squirrel picture site.

So keep your anchor text as detailed as possible to boost link relevancy.

 

4. Ratio is not Everything Always

 

No discernible association could be discovered with or without phrase matching, partial matching, or randomness.

That is primarily due to Google’s sophisticated AI models, which allow the search engine to examine a website’s whole meaning and anchor text.

Obviously, rather than just one piece of anchor text on its own.

If you want to spend your time as efficiently as possible, do not bother tinkering with a site’s anchor-text ratio.

To be noticed by Google’s algorithms, it’s best to keep your efforts minimum.

 

5. Never Forget About Your Image

 

You are missing out on many benefits if you do not have them.

They aid visually challenged readers in their comprehension of a picture.

Besides serving as anchor text, picture anchor texts inform Google algorithms about the content of an image.

For tags to be effective; they need to be very descriptive and grammatically correct.

It used to be standard practice to overuse keywords in image tags, but Google swiftly nipped it in the bud.

Choose a primary term, match keywords, and combine it into a particular image-descriptive statement.

 

Now let’s dive into something you may badly need when you go for an anchor text optimization in SEO.

It is none other than:

Anchor Text Optimization and Google Penguin Updates

 

Anchor text commonly uses SEO-optimized keywords.

Use “mobile app” and “mobile developer” as anchor text on other websites to rank for such keywords.

In anticipation of Penguin, avoid over-optimizing anchor text.

Let’s examine!

 

Quality Trumps Quantity

 

Google needs to know these keywords from your web pages.

Ten connections from trustworthy sites are worth more than 30 from low-quality ones.

We will explore brand-related connections’ purpose and implementation.

 

Use Brand Names

 

Get backlinks or link anchors to your brand’s name to gain from its “known” status.

If a fan of your products or brand blogs about them, they’ll link to your URL or business name.

Here external links and internal links both need to be used carefully. 

 

Anchor Text Variations

 

Never use keywords or brand names as anchor text.

Mix phrases for natural variety.

Use phrases like “Click here” or “Find out more” in addition to brand terms and optimized keywords.

 

Be Careful with Mage Anchors

 

Your site is adrift on the internet; thus, building backlinks is crucial.

So your keyword-optimized anchor text is constantly on your mind.

Penguin is looking for sites that “overdo” anchor text.

It is permissible to utilize trademark words and modify anchor text to give Google signals.

 

Avoid overdoing it

post_content:
B2B SEO is search engine optimization for companies that sell to other companies. The aim is simple: when a business buyer searches for a problem you solve, your pages appear, answer the question and lead to an enquiry.

This guide explains what B2B SEO is, how it differs from consumer SEO, and how to build a B2B SEO strategy in eight steps. It also covers keywords, content, links, AI search, measurement and common mistakes. If you are thinking of hiring help, read our guide to B2B SEO agencies too.

What is B2B SEO?

B2B SEO is the practice of improving a business-to-business website so it ranks in Google and appears in AI answers for the searches your buyers make. That covers your pages, your technical setup, your links from other sites and the content that answers buyer questions.

The goal is not traffic for its own sake. It is qualified enquiries: people who match your customer profile and are likely to talk to sales.

How is B2B SEO different from B2C SEO?

B2B SEOB2C SEO
Who buysSeveral people in a company: users, managers, finance, leadersUsually one person or household
Sales cycleWeeks or months, with many searches along the wayOften short, sometimes one visit
Search volumeOften small and specializedOften large and broad
Content neededDetailed guides, comparisons, case studies and proofProduct pages, reviews, short guides
Main goalQualified leads and pipelineSales or sign-ups
Success measureEnquiries, demos, deals influenced by searchOrders and revenue

The biggest difference is the buying group. A page may be read by the person who will use your product, by the manager who approves it and by the person who checks the contract. Each asks different questions, so your content must cover all three.

Why is SEO important for B2B companies?

  • Buyers research before they talk to you. They read, compare and shortlist on their own. If you are not in the results, you are not on the shortlist.
  • It reaches people at the right moment. A search is a stated need, unlike an ad that interrupts.
  • It builds assets. A strong page keeps working for months or years.
  • It supports sales. Good content answers questions your team gets on every call.
  • It supports AI search visibility. The same clear, trusted pages are what AI tools pull from when buyers ask for options.

SEO is slow. Google says changes can take from a few hours to several months to show. Plan for a program of six to twelve months, not a quick campaign.

B2B SEO strategy: 8 steps

Step 1: Define your buyers

List the people involved in a purchase. For each, write their job, their main problem and the questions they ask before they buy. Use sales calls, support tickets and customer interviews, not guesses.

RoleWhat they care aboutQuestions they search
UserWill it work for my tasks?how to do [task], [product type] features
ManagerWill it save time and money?best [product type] for [team size], [product] vs [competitor]
Finance or procurementWhat does it cost and what are the terms?[product] pricing, [product] contract length
LeaderIs it safe and will it grow with us?[product] security, [product] case study

Step 2: Set goals tied to the business

Choose goals that sales and finance care about. Examples: demo requests from organic search, enquiries from a named industry, or share of leads from search. Track traffic as a means, not the goal.

Step 3: Run an audit

An SEO audit shows where you stand. Check:

  • Technical health. Can search engines crawl and index your key pages? Is the site fast and secure?
  • Content. Which pages bring visits and enquiries? Which are thin or out of date?
  • Keywords. What do you already rank for, and where are the gaps?
  • Links. Who links to you, and how does that compare with your rivals?
  • Competitors. Who ranks for your key searches?

Step 4: Do keyword research by buyer stage

Map keywords to the path a buyer takes. Include small searches. In B2B, a search made 30 times a month by the right buyers can beat one made 3,000 times a month by the wrong audience.

StageExample searchPage to build
Problem awarewhy do invoices get paid lateA guide that explains the causes and fixes
Solution awareinvoice automation software for agenciesA solution page for that industry
Comparing[your product] vs [competitor]A fair comparison page
Ready to buy[your product] pricingA pricing or "how we price" page
Needs proofinvoice automation case studyA case study with real results

The examples above are illustrative. Use your own market terms and check volume and difficulty in a keyword tool. Read the top results to make sure your page matches the type of page that ranks.

Step 5: Build the right pages

Most B2B sites need these page types:

  • Product or service pages. One for each offer, written for the buyer's problem.
  • Industry pages. One for each sector you serve, with its own examples.
  • Use-case pages. Show how the product solves a specific task.
  • Guides and explainers. Answer questions at the top of the funnel.
  • Comparison and alternative pages. Be fair and factual.
  • Case studies. Real clients, real results, with their permission.
  • Pricing or how we price. Buyers look for it, so say something useful.

Write each page to answer one main question completely. Add real examples, numbers you can source, and names of the experts behind the page.

Step 6: Show experience, expertise and trust (E-E-A-T)

Google's guidance on helpful content asks whether a page shows first-hand experience, expertise, authority and trust. For B2B this means:

  • Named authors with real job titles and short bios
  • Examples from your own work and customers
  • Clear sources for facts and statistics
  • A visible "last updated" date
  • Reviews, client logos you have permission to show, and security or compliance details where they matter

Step 7: Fix technical SEO and structure

  • Crawl and indexing. Make sure important pages can be found and indexed. Use a sitemap and check Search Console for errors.
  • Speed and mobile. Buyers often read on a phone between meetings.
  • Site structure. Group pages by topic and link them so buyers and search engines can follow the path.
  • Titles and headings. Use the words buyers use, near the start.
  • Schema markup. Add structured data for your organization, articles, FAQs and products where it applies.
  • International setup. If you sell in several countries, use the right language and region markup.

Step 8: Earn links and mentions

Links from trusted sites help your pages rank. In B2B, good sources are industry bodies, trade press, partner and customer sites, podcasts, conference pages and respected blogs. Ways to earn them:

  • Publish original data from your own work
  • Offer expert quotes to journalists and writers
  • Build a free tool or template people want to share
  • Write guest articles for relevant sites
  • Collect links from partners and clients who already know you

Do not buy links. Google's spam policies list buying or selling links for ranking purposes as link spam.

A worked example: a software company that sells to accountants

This example is illustrative. It shows how the steps fit together.

StepWhat the company decides
BuyersPractice owners (decide), senior accountants (use), the office manager (budget)
Goal20 demo requests a month from organic search within 12 months
Audit resultStrong blog, no pricing page, no industry pages, slow mobile pages
KeywordsSolution searches such as "client onboarding software for accountants" and comparison searches
PagesThree solution pages, one pricing page, five comparison pages, two case studies
TrustNamed authors, a security page, a client quote with permission
LinksGuest articles on two accounting blogs, a listing with a professional body
MeasureDemo requests by landing page, tracked monthly with the CRM

The company reviews after three months. Comparison pages and the pricing page bring the first demo requests. The blog brings visits but few enquiries. The plan shifts toward more bottom-of-funnel pages. That is the loop: plan, publish, measure, adjust.

What types of B2B keywords should you target?

Group your keywords by what the searcher wants. Each type needs a different page.

TypeWhat the searcher wantsExampleBest page
InformationalTo learnwhat is supply chain visibilityGuide or explainer
CommercialTo compare optionsbest supply chain software for manufacturersComparison, list or solution page
TransactionalTo actsupply chain software demoProduct page with a clear call to action
NavigationalTo find a brand[your brand] loginHome page, login and support pages
Problem-basedTo fix a painhow to reduce late shipmentsGuide that leads to your solution

Do not write one page for all five. A guide that tries to sell, compare and teach at once ranks for none of them.

How do you build topic clusters in B2B?

A topic cluster is a group of pages on one subject. One main page covers the topic broadly, and several support pages cover parts of it in detail. All of them link to each other. This shows search engines and buyers that you know the subject well.

For example, a company that sells payment software for marketplaces could build a cluster like this:

  • Main page: marketplace payments, a complete guide
  • Support pages: how split payments work, marketplace payout schedules, fraud checks for marketplaces, how to choose a payment provider, marketplace payments compared with standard card payments
  • Proof pages: one case study and one product page that the cluster links to

Start with the clusters closest to what you sell. Build one well before you start the next.

What content formats work in B2B SEO?

Pick the format that fits the question.

  • Guides. For broad questions that need depth, such as "how to choose" or "how to set up."
  • Checklists and templates. Easy to use and to link to. Good for lead capture if the value is real.
  • Comparison pages. For buyers weighing two options. State the facts and be fair about where a rival is better.
  • Case studies. A client's problem, what you did and the result in real numbers, with permission to share.
  • Glossary pages. Short, clear answers to "what is" searches.
  • Original research. Data from your own work that others cite and link to.
  • Video and webinars. Useful for demos and expert talks. Add a written summary so the content can be found.

How does technical SEO apply to B2B sites?

Many B2B sites have a large product catalog, gated content, several languages or a complicated structure. That creates common technical problems:

ProblemWhy it hurtsFix
Key pages not indexedThey cannot rankCheck Search Console, fix blocks and add internal links
Gated contentSearch engines cannot read itShow a useful summary or the full text, and gate only extras
Duplicate pagesPages compete with each otherMerge them or set a clear canonical page
Slow, heavy pagesVisitors leaveCompress images, limit scripts, use caching
Poor internal linksImportant pages look unimportantLink from related pages with clear link text
Wrong region or language setupThe wrong country page appearsUse proper language and region markup

How long does B2B SEO take?

Google says some changes show in hours and others take months, and it suggests waiting a few weeks before you judge a change. B2B adds a second delay: the sales cycle. A page may rank within months and the deal it influences may close months after that.

A reasonable expectation is:

  • Months 1 to 3: audit, fixes, keyword plan and first pages
  • Months 4 to 6: early rankings for smaller searches and the first enquiries
  • Months 7 to 12: growth in rankings, more pages and clearer data on leads

These ranges are a planning guide, not a promise. Your market, site and effort change the pace.

How much does B2B SEO cost?

There is no standard price. It depends on the size of your site, how competitive your market is, how much content you need and how much your team does. The cost has three parts: people (your team, a freelancer or an agency), tools (keyword, audit and reporting software) and content and links (writing, design and outreach).

When you compare quotes, compare the scope. A low price may not include writing, links or reporting. Ask what you get each month and how it ties to enquiries.

A 90-day plan to start

DaysWorkResult
1 to 14Buyer research, goals, audit of technical health, content and linksA clear starting point and a list of fixes
15 to 30Fix the biggest technical problems; set up tracking from search to CRMClean site and data you can trust
31 to 60Keyword map; write or rewrite the 3 to 5 pages closest to sales: solution, comparison, pricingPages that can bring ready-to-buy enquiries
61 to 90Publish two guides; start link outreach; review results and set the next 90 daysA repeatable monthly routine

Do not try to publish dozens of pages at once. A steady pace with checked, useful pages is safer than a burst of thin ones.

How do you choose between focusing on SaaS, services or manufacturing?

The approach changes slightly by sector.

  • B2B software (SaaS): focus on use cases, integrations, comparisons and "alternative to" searches. Free trials and demos are the main conversions.
  • Professional services: focus on expertise. Named experts, case studies and guides by topic build trust. Conversions are enquiries and calls.
  • Manufacturing and industrial: focus on product specifications, applications, standards and supplier searches. Clear data sheets and catalog pages matter.
  • Healthcare and life sciences: focus on accuracy, sources and compliance. Review claims carefully before you publish.

How should B2B SEO handle AI search?

Buyers now ask AI tools such as ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI answers for vendor ideas and explanations. These tools pull from pages that are clear, factual and well sourced. To fit:

  • Put a short, direct answer at the top of each page.
  • Use clear headings, lists and tables.
  • Keep facts consistent across your site, profiles and listings.
  • Be specific about who you serve and what you do. Vague copy gives AI nothing to repeat.
  • Earn independent mentions in reviews, press and partner pages.
  • Check what AI tools say about you. Ask them your buyers' questions and note where you are missing or wrong.

No method guarantees a mention. The steps above also help normal search, so they are worth doing either way.

How do you measure B2B SEO?

Measure what the business cares about. A simple set:

  • Organic traffic to pages that matter, not all pages
  • Rankings for a short list of key searches
  • Conversions: demo requests, contact forms, downloads and calls from organic search
  • Lead quality: the share that sales accepts
  • Pipeline and revenue influenced by search, tracked in your CRM
  • Search Console data: impressions, clicks and the searches that bring them

Because B2B deals are slow, a lead from search may close months later. Connect your analytics to your CRM so you can trace a deal back to its first search visit.

How do you run a B2B SEO audit?

A B2B SEO audit is a structured check of your site and search presence. You can do a first pass yourself in a day. Use this order:

  1. Check indexing. In Search Console, see how many pages are indexed and why others are not. Compare with the pages you want to rank.
  2. List your top pages. Which pages bring visits and which bring enquiries? Often they are different pages.
  3. Find gaps. Search your 10 most important buyer questions in Google. Note who ranks and what type of page it is.
  4. Review page quality. For each key page, ask if it answers the question fully, names the author, shows proof and has a clear next step.
  5. Check links. See who links to you and to your three closest rivals. Look for sources that link to them but not to you.
  6. Test speed and mobile. Open your key pages on a phone and note slow or broken parts.
  7. Write the fix list. Sort it into quick fixes, pages to build and long-term work.

Keep the audit as a living file. Update it each quarter so you can see progress.

How do you work with sales on B2B SEO?

Sales teams hear the exact words buyers use. Use them.

  • Ask sales for the top 20 questions buyers ask in first calls and write a page for each.
  • Collect objections. "How do you compare with X?" and "Is it secure?" are page ideas.
  • Share new pages with sales so they can send them to buyers. A page that helps in a call often ranks well too.
  • Ask sales to tag the source of every lead, so you can see which search pages helped.
  • Meet monthly for 30 minutes to review leads from search and decide what to write next.

In-house or agency?

Small teams often start in-house with one marketer and a freelance writer. Larger programs may need an agency for strategy, writing, technical work and reporting. Many companies mix both: the agency sets the plan and the in-house team supplies product knowledge. Ask for a written scope, who writes the content, how results tie to leads and how you can end the contract.

Common B2B SEO mistakes

  • Chasing traffic. Visits from the wrong audience do not become enquiries.
  • Writing only top-of-funnel posts. Buyers near a decision need comparison, pricing and proof pages.
  • Skipping the buying group. Content for users only misses the people who approve.
  • Thin or generic pages. "We offer solutions" tells nobody anything.
  • No proof. Claims without case studies, names or numbers do not convince.
  • Ignoring technical health. Pages that are not indexed cannot rank.
  • Expecting fast results. Plan for months.
  • Never updating. Old pages lose ground. Refresh key pages at least once a year.

A quick checklist

  • Buyers and their questions written down
  • Goals tied to leads and pipeline
  • An audit of technical health, content, keywords and links
  • Keywords mapped to each buyer stage
  • Pages for products, industries, use cases, comparisons, pricing and proof
  • Named authors, sources and a last-updated date on each page
  • Honest link building
  • Reports that tie search to enquiries and deals

Final thoughts

B2B SEO works when it follows the way your buyers actually buy. Know who is involved, answer their questions at each stage and prove your claims. Then measure leads, not only visits, and improve the pages that move deals forward.

post_content:
A B2B SEO agency helps a business that sells to other businesses get found in search. Good ones bring in qualified leads (qualified enquiries) from buyers who search for months before they speak to sales. Poor ones bring in traffic that never turns into pipeline.

This guide explains what B2B SEO is, what an agency does, how much it can cost, and how to choose one. It ends with questions to ask before you sign and mistakes to avoid.

What is B2B SEO?

B2B SEO is search engine optimization for companies that sell to other companies. The goal is to help the right people find you when they search for a problem you solve.

It differs from consumer SEO in three ways:

  • The sales cycle is long. Buyers research for weeks or months and compare several vendors.
  • Several people decide. The person who uses your product is often not the person who approves the purchase.
  • Small searches can be worth a lot. A search used by 50 people a month can bring more pipeline than one used by 5,000, if those 50 are ready to buy.

That is why B2B guides tell you to measure lead generation and pipeline, not only organic traffic and rankings.

What is a B2B SEO agency?

A B2B SEO agency is a specialized marketing agency that plans and runs search work for business-to-business brands, from B2B SaaS companies to enterprise manufacturers. It may do the work for you, or set the plan and standards for your own team. Many also cover AI search, which is how your brand appears in tools such as ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews. The work behind it is often called generative engine optimization (GEO).

What is a B2B SEO strategy?

A B2B SEO strategy is the plan an agency builds for you. It decides which searches to win, which pages to create or fix, and how each page helps a buyer move from first question to purchase. A good B2B SEO strategy is built on the funnel: the path a buyer takes from awareness, to comparing options, to a decision.

It rests on five parts:

  • Buyer research. Who the decision-makers are, what they ask and where they look. For a larger company, there may be a user, a manager and a person who signs off.
  • An SEO audit. A check of your site's technical health, content and competitors. This sets the starting point and finds quick wins.
  • A content plan. Pages and articles matched to each stage of the funnel, including thought leadership: original views and experience from your own experts.
  • Technical foundations. Fast pages, clean structure and structured data (schema) so search engines understand what each page is about.
  • Attribution. A way to trace conversions back to the page and search that brought them in, so you can see what produces revenue.

When an agency shows you its approach, check that all five are there. A plan that is only a list of keywords is not a strategy.

What do B2B SEO services include?

Most agencies offer the same core services. The difference is how well they do each one.

ServiceWhat it is
Keyword researchFinding the searches your buyers make at each stage, from first question to vendor comparison
Content strategy and writingSEO content and content marketing: guides, comparison pages and answers to buyer questions, written with real expert input
Technical SEOMaking sure search engines can crawl, read and index your site, and that it loads fast. This includes international SEO if you sell in several markets
On-page optimizationTitles, headings, links and structure that show each page's purpose
Link building and digital PREarning mentions and links from trusted sites, without buying them
Conversion workLanding pages and forms that turn visitors into enquiries
ReportingTying search results to leads and revenue in your customer system
AI search visibilityTracking and improving how AI tools describe and cite your brand

What does a B2B SEO engagement look like, step by step?

Knowing the process helps you spot an agency that is making it up as it goes. Most good engagements follow the same path. The dates below are typical, not promises.

  1. Discovery (weeks 1 to 2). The agency learns your product, your buyers and your sales process. It asks for access to Google Search Console, your analytics and, ideally, your customer system. You share your best customers and your lost deals.
  2. Audit (weeks 2 to 4). It checks your site's technical health, your current content and your competitors. The output is a written list of problems and opportunities, ranked by effort and impact.
  3. Strategy (weeks 3 to 5). It turns the audit into a plan: which buyer questions to answer first, which pages to fix, which to create, and what to stop. You agree the goals and the numbers that will show progress.
  4. Foundations (months 1 to 3). Technical fixes ship, key pages are rewritten and tracking is set up so results can be tied to leads.
  5. Content and authority (months 2 to 6 and on). New content goes live on a steady schedule. The agency earns links and mentions from trusted sites.
  6. Reporting and review (every month). You get a short report of what was done, what moved and what is next. Every quarter the plan is checked against your business goals.

If an agency cannot describe its process in this much detail, ask again. A vague answer usually means the work is vague.

How much does a B2B SEO agency cost?

There is no standard price. It depends on the size of your site, how competitive your market is, how much content you need and how much your own team does.

Published prices vary a lot. For example, one agency lists prices from $9,000 a month for its integrated B2B program, and another lists tiers from $3,000 to $68,250 a month. These are the agencies' own figures, so treat them as examples of the range, not as a benchmark.

Three things drive the price: how many pages and topics are in scope, whether the agency writes the content or advises your writers, and whether technical fixes and link work are included. Ask for a written scope and a price that matches it. Be careful with a low price that does not say what you get.

At Reinforce Lab, our SEO and AI search work is scoped after a free diagnostic. Packages start from $5,000 setup, and the packages page shows the tiers.

How long does B2B SEO take to work?

Google says some changes take a few hours and others take several months. It suggests waiting a few weeks before judging whether a change helped. B2B sales cycles are long too, so a page may be found in a few months but only lead to a deal later.

Be wary of any agency that promises a ranking date or a number-one position. Nobody controls Google's results.

Is SEO effective for B2B?

Yes, when it is built around how business buyers search. Buyers look for answers before they talk to a sales rep. If your pages answer their questions, you are present when they compare options. SEO also keeps working after the work is done, unlike paid ads that stop when you stop paying.

It works poorly when it chases traffic. Pages that rank for broad terms but never speak to a buyer's problem do not create pipeline.

An example: how B2B keyword research differs

This example is made up to show the idea. It is not a real client result.

Imagine a company that sells inventory software to wholesale distributors. A weak agency starts with the biggest search it can find, such as "inventory management". Many people search it, but most are students, shop owners or people who want a free spreadsheet. Very few can buy.

A good B2B agency starts with the buyer's journey instead:

Buyer stageExample searchPage to create
Knows the problemwhy do we run out of stock on fast-selling itemsA guide that explains the causes and fixes
Looking at solutionsinventory software for wholesale distributorsA solution page for distributors
Comparing vendors[your product] vs [competitor]A fair comparison page
Ready to buy[your product] pricingA clear pricing or "how we price" page
Needs proofinventory software case study distributionA case study with real results

The searches near the bottom of the table are small. They are also the ones where a visitor is closest to a decision. Ask any agency to show you a table like this for your own business before you sign.

How does B2B SEO differ by sector?

"B2B" covers very different businesses. An agency that is strong in one sector may be weak in another. Here is how the work changes:

  • Software and technology. Buyers compare products closely. Comparison pages, integration pages and clear documentation matter, and the site must be readable by search crawlers even if it relies on JavaScript. See our page on B2B SaaS.
  • Manufacturing and industrial. Buyers are engineers and specifiers. They search for specifications, applications and part numbers. Product data and technical content must be exact. See manufacturing.
  • Professional services. Trust decides the sale. Pages for each practice area and each expert, backed by clear author details, do the work. See professional services.
  • Pharma and healthcare. Claims must be accurate and reviewed. Content passes medical or legal review before it is published, so the agency must plan around your approval cycle. See pharmaceutical and life sciences.
  • Education. Buyers include institutions as well as students. Course and programme pages must be clear and easy to find. See education.

When you speak to agencies, ask which of these they have done and what they changed for their clients.

How is B2B SEO different from paid search?

Paid search, or pay-per-click advertising, puts your ad in front of buyers as soon as you pay. It stops when the budget stops. SEO takes longer to start, but the pages keep working after the work is done. Many B2B companies use both: paid search for fast tests and key terms, and SEO for lasting visibility. A good agency should be able to say how the two fit together, and what each one costs you per qualified lead.

How do you choose a B2B SEO agency?

Several guides, including ones from agencies that sell this service, give the same advice. Use these seven checks.

1. Start with your sales process

Before you look at agencies, write down how your buyers find you, who decides, and what a good lead is. Then judge each agency on how well it fits that, not on its list of services.

2. Look for B2B and niche experience

Some agencies are full-service marketing agencies. Others specialize in one sector or one kind of work. Both can be good. What matters is proof that they have done your kind of work.

A software company, a manufacturer and a law firm all sell to businesses, but their buyers search very differently. Ask for work in your sector or a close one, and for a track record you can check. An agency that knows your buyers writes better content and needs less of your time.

3. Check who writes the content

Ask who writes, who edits and where the expertise comes from. Google asks whether content is mass-produced or outsourced to many creators so that no page gets real care. Its other questions are a good test: does it give original information, clear sourcing, and was it written or reviewed by someone who knows the topic?

4. Ask how they report results

Reviews from past clients help here. Ask for two or three references you can call, and ask what the agency did, how they worked together and what changed.

The best reports connect organic search to leads, opportunities and revenue in your customer system. A report with only rankings and traffic hides what you most need to know.

5. Test their technical depth

B2B sites often have gated content, many languages or complex menus. Ask how the agency finds crawl and index problems, and who fixes them.

6. Ask about links and AI search

Ask how they earn links. Google's spam policies say buying or selling links for ranking purposes, and using automated programs to create links, are link spam. An agency that cannot explain its method clearly is a risk. Also ask how it tracks your brand in AI answers, because buyers now use those tools too.

7. Get a written scope, price and exit terms

You should know what is included, how much it costs, how long the contract runs and how you can leave. Make a shortlist of three or four agencies and compare them on the same questions.

Should you choose a large agency or a smaller one?

Large agencies offer many services and strong tools, but your account may be handled by junior staff. Smaller firms often give you direct access to senior people but may cover fewer services. Neither is better by itself. Ask who will actually do your work, and meet them before you sign.

Should you hire an agency or build an in-house team?

An in-house team knows your product best and works only for you. An agency brings a full set of skills at once: strategy, writing, technical work and reporting. Many companies use both. The agency sets the strategy and standards, and the in-house team supplies product knowledge and approves content.

How to compare agencies with a scorecard

After the first calls, a simple scorecard keeps the choice fair. List your criteria down the side. Score each agency from 1 to 5 in each row, and write one line of evidence for every score. Give the criteria that matter most to you more weight.

CriterionAgency AAgency BAgency C
Experience in your sector (check references)425
Who writes the content344
Reporting tied to leads and revenue524
Technical depth433
Link method and AI search coverage324
Clear scope, price and exit terms435
Total231625

The numbers above are made up. The point is the method: Agency B looks cheaper, but it scores low where it matters most. A scorecard makes that visible before you spend a cent.

What to put in your brief to an agency

A good brief gets you good proposals. Send each agency the same one. Include:

  • Your business: what you sell, who buys and how long a sale takes.
  • Your goal: for example, 20 percent more qualified enquiries in six months.
  • Your current state: your site, your recent search results and what you have tried.
  • Your constraints: budget range, who can approve content and who can change the site.
  • What you want back: a plan, a scope, a price, and examples of similar work.

What should a monthly SEO report show?

Ask to see a sample report before you sign. A useful one has five parts:

  1. What we did: the fixes shipped and the pages published or updated.
  2. What moved: impressions, clicks and rankings for the searches that matter to buyers.
  3. What it brought: enquiries and opportunities from organic search, traced in your customer system.
  4. What we learned: what worked, what did not and why.
  5. What is next: the plan for the coming month, and anything the agency needs from you.

A report that is only a chart of traffic is not enough.

How do you work with an agency once you have chosen one?

The choice is only half the job. These habits help the work go well:

  • Name one owner on your side. Someone who can answer questions and approve work in days, not weeks.
  • Give access early. Search Console, analytics and your customer system are needed in the first week.
  • Share your sales knowledge. Your sales team hears the questions buyers ask. Pass them on.
  • Review content for accuracy. Your experts should check every claim before it is published.
  • Meet on a fixed schedule. A short monthly call beats ad hoc emails.
  • Review at 90 days. Check progress against the plan. If the foundations are not in place by then, ask why.

Questions to ask a B2B SEO agency before you hire

  • How do you do keyword research for a company like ours?
  • Can you show work for companies in our sector, and what did it change?
  • Who writes the content, and how do you get our experts' knowledge?
  • How will you connect search results to our leads and revenue?
  • How do you earn links, and will you ever buy them?
  • How do you track and improve our visibility in AI answers?
  • Who will work on our account, and how often will we meet?
  • What is included in the price, and how can we end the contract?

What should the contract cover?

Read the agreement before you sign, and ask for changes if something is unclear. Look for these points:

  • Scope: a written list of what is included and what is not.
  • Price and payment: what you pay, when, and what extra work costs.
  • Term and exit: how long it runs and how you can leave. Check any minimum term.
  • Ownership: you should own the content, the accounts and the data produced for you.
  • Access: the agency should use accounts in your name, so you keep everything if you leave.
  • Reporting: what you will receive and how often.
  • Methods: a promise to follow Google's guidelines and not to buy links.

What are the warning signs of a poor B2B SEO agency?

  • It guarantees a ranking or a date for page one.
  • It cannot explain how it earns links.
  • It sends the same plan to every client.
  • It will not show a sample report or name a reference.
  • It reports traffic only.
  • It asks you to sign a long contract before it has seen your site.
  • It refuses to use accounts in your name.
  • It sells you a long list of keywords instead of a plan.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Choosing on price alone. A cheap plan that delivers nothing is the most expensive one.
  • Trusting a ranked list from an agency. Many "best agency" lists are written by agencies that rank themselves first. Use them to build a shortlist, then check references and case studies yourself.
  • Accepting a ranking guarantee. Nobody can promise a number-one position.
  • Judging by traffic. Ask for enquiries and pipeline.
  • Skipping the questions above. The answers tell you more than a sales deck.

Wrapping up

Choose a B2B SEO agency that understands your buyers, shows who does the work, reports in leads and revenue, and gives you a clear written scope. Take your time: a wrong choice costs months.

How to Use Beaver Builder To Build a Website In WordPress?

 

Beaver Builder is a website builder that allows users to create custom websites and pages using a drag-and-drop interface.

 

Step 01: Installing Beaver Builder on Your WordPress Site

 

Installing Beaver Builder is the first step in using this website builder to create custom pages and websites. This step involves installing the Beaver Builder plugin on your WordPress site.

Here’s how it works:
  1. Log in to WordPress dashboard or your WordPress site’s administration area.
  2. Navigate to the “Plugins” section and click on “Add New.”
  3. In the search bar, type “Beaver Builder” and click the “Search Plugins” button.
  4. Select the “Beaver Builder” plugin and click the “Install Now” button.
  5. Once the plugin is installed, click the “Activate” button to start using Beaver Builder.
  6. After activating the plugin, you will see a new “Beaver Builder” menu item in the WordPress administration area.
  7. To build your website with Beaver Builder, simply click the “Beaver Builder” menu item and select “Page Builder.“

This process is straightforward and can be completed in just a few minutes. Once the plugin is installed, you’re ready to start using Beaver Builder to create custom pages and websites for your WordPress site.

 

Step 2: Add Your New Page

 

Adding Your New Page in Beaver Builder is the second step in creating a custom page using this website builder. Here’s how it works:

  1. Navigate to the “Beaver Builder” menu item.
  2. Click on “Page Builder” to access the Beaver Builder interface.
  3. Click the “Add New” button to create a new page.
  4. Enter a title for your new page and select a template to use as a starting point for your design, or start with a blank page.
  5. Click the “Launch Page Builder” button to start building your page.
  6. The Beaver Builder interface will load, and you will be able to use the drag-and-drop interface to add, edit, and rearrange elements on your page.
  7. You can add text, images, buttons, and other elements to your page using the various modules available in Beaver Builder.
  8. Once you’re finished designing your page, you can preview it to see how it will look on different devices, such as desktops, laptops, tablets, and smartphones.
  9. When you’re satisfied with your design, you can save and publish your page to make it live on the web.

This process is straightforward and intuitive, making it easy for users of all skill levels to create custom pages with Beaver Builder.

The drag-and-drop interface and extensive customization options make it a popular choice for those looking to create custom pages and websites for their WordPress site.

 

Sign Up Now

Step 3: Choose a Page Template in Beaver Builder

 

Choosing a Template in Beaver Builder is an optional step in the process of creating a custom page or website. Here’s how it works:

  1. Navigate to the “Beaver Builder” menu item.
  2. Click on “Page Builder” to access the Beaver Builder interface.
  3. If you’re starting a new page, click the “Add New” button and enter a title for your page.
  4. To choose a template, click the “Templates” tab in the Beaver Builder interface.
  5. Browse through the available templates to find one that matches the look and feel you’re going for. Templates are categorized by type, such as landing pages, homepages, and more.
  6. Click on a template to preview it.
  7. If you find a template that you like, click the “Use Template” button to select it.
  8. The template will be added to your page, and you will be able to use the drag-and-drop interface to edit and customize it to your liking.
  9. You can also start with a blank page and build your design from scratch if you prefer.

Templates are a great starting point for a website designer who is looking for inspiration or wants to get a website up and running quickly. By choosing a template, you can get a professional-looking website with minimal effort.

Once you have a template in place, you can use Beaver Builder’s drag-and-drop interface to customize it to your liking.

 

Step 4: Rearrange the Layout with Columns and Prebuilt Rows

 

Rearranging the Layout with Columns and Prebuilt Rows in Beaver Builder is a key step in creating a custom page or website. Here’s how it works:

  1. If you’ve chosen a template, you will see a pre-designed layout that you can customize to your liking.
  2. To rearrange the layout, use the drag-and-drop interface to add, edit, and rearrange columns and prebuilt rows.
  3. Beaver Builder provides a variety of column and row templates that you can use to create a custom layout for your page.
  4. To add a new row, click the “Add Row” button and select the type of row you want to add, such as a full-width row or a multi-column row.
  5. Once you’ve added a row, you can add modules, such as text, images, buttons, and more, to fill the columns.
  6. You can also adjust the number of columns in a row and the width of each column to create a custom layout that meets your needs.
  7. To rearrange elements on your page, simply drag and drop them to the desired location.

This step is critical in creating a custom page or website that meets your needs and provides a great user experience.

With the flexibility to add and rearrange columns and prebuilt rows, Beaver Builder makes it easy to create a custom layout that fits your brand and add content to it.

 

Step 5: Add Additional Modules

 

Adding Additional Modules in Beaver Builder is the process of adding new elements to your page to make it more dynamic and engaging. Here’s how it works:

  1. Select the page that you want to add modules to.

post_content:
Food copywriting is a really fun gig for modern times. Observing some of the best examples of great food copywriting can help you stay ahead.

Ever since there has been marketing for food, copywriting has played a major part in making a good food product great, and a great food product incredible.

So this article is to help you find some best food copywriting and food marketing copywriting examples.

Food copywriting entails a large and versatile section of food marketing. People eat not just to live, but to be delighted as well.

So food writing or examples of food copywriting is everywhere.

From menu description examples to food description examples, food copywriting can be seen all around us.

We also witness written food advertisement examples on many of our social media platforms and webpages.

These are responsible for a lot of traffic in online cutlery services or rise of customers in popular restaurants.

With that explained, let us dive deep into what food copywriting truly is.

 

What is Food Copywriting?

 

Food copywriting is basically writing about food, but in a commercial form for marketing purposes.

As copywriting means writing for advertisements to generate sales, food copywriting does the same for food.

It is basically food writing or food content writing. What you like about food is possibly what maximum people who have an appetite like as well. 

In terms of modern writing gigs, food writing or food copywriting has a universal appeal, if done right.

Getting paid to enjoy food and reviewing it, what could be better if you are a food lover, right?

With that in mind, you can surely look into a few tips and tricks that would make you the best food copywriter people would be pleased to hire.

Food copywriting can be done with a lot of creativity and precision.

Whether your targeted business is totally based on online catering, or a physical place like a restaurant, or café, your conscious and intuitive writing can take it to another level.

So, you can use some good food copywriting examples for reference.

Here are some of the best examples of great food copywriting for your consideration.

 

Best Examples of Great Food Copywriting

 

The best examples of great food copywriting can be found lying around our roads or the websites where we roam.

It is there in every witty food advertisement writings to every slogan created by popular food brands.

So how do these restaurants, brands, pages, or websites keep up these great examples of copywriting samples every week or month or so?

Let us point out some of the key factors and practices to generate effective food copywriting.

 

1. Descriptive Keywords for your target audience

 

First of all, your writing should definitely appeal to the readers’ five senses.

Start by pointing out the name of the dish or restaurant you are writing about. 

Make sure you use the long tail keyword for it, as it already paints a description in the readers’ minds.

As a food reviewer or food copywriter, you must already have an idea about what vocabularies create what kind of images.

You must appeal to the visual, olfactory, and gustatory senses while writing about your food.

Of course, most of the times, the name of the item or recipe itself can appeal to these senses.

However, you should not miss the opportunity to put your own spin and own two cents on the description of the items in your website details or menu details.

 

2. Use of Numbers

 

Numbers in your written copy drive your points across more impactfully and immediately.

Additionally, numbers are eye-catchy. On a page full of texts, numbers catch the most immediate attention.

Streamline your food copywriting with numbered bullet points where you can.

You can number the ingredients in order of use or importance for your copywriting.

Otherwise if you want to overview the appetizing cooking process, you can describe it through numbered bullet points to further titillate your audience as they wait to grab hold of the food and put it in their watered mouth.

 

3. Less Is More

 

In terms of descriptions, less is more. Do not think about writing full-sentence descriptions everywhere. Play with your consumers’ imagination.

Shortly let your audience know where your food comes from in your menu description.

Visualize the beginnings, and let your customer visualize the end as they savor the taste of the food you are going to promote.

 

4. Use Humor

 

Using lighthearted writing is always a plus for you as a food copywriter.

It gives off the sense that you know how to tickle the sense of humor of your audience.

Of course be discrete in describing the taste, smell, and texture of the food.

However, also play around with words when you can. Use alliterations, rhythms, and rhymes to enrich the flow of your copy writing.

For example, if you write “Munch More with Meaty Monster!” as ad copywriting for one of your meaty burger item, you can say it is quite catchy and has good use of alliterations, using M’s at the beginning of consecutive words.

This is just an example of rhythmic catchiness you can include in your copywriting.

There are tons of humorous food copywriting examples out there. We will wait to see what your funny bones come up with!

 

5. Be Conversational

 

Everyone eats food, and almost everyone has an opinion about it.

Whether which dish is great, which ambiance they like, or which type of recipe they prefer, you can give your audience a chance to interact.

Most importantly, it will give your audience a notion of customization.

They will obviously feel like they are being heard and valued.

You can do it powerfully through your copywriting.

Now you move on to your product description, which is your food, or restaurant.

Based on whether you are writing to review a restaurant, food products, or food brands, your copywriting examples will be a bit different.

Let us talk about restaurant copywriting examples first.

 

6. Copywriting for Restaurants

 

There are a lot of restaurant review websites you can follow who are masters at appetizing potential customers.

Some customers might be looking for exquisite delicacies. Some might be looking for a proper place to satiate their hunger where the price is cheaper and affordable.

Regardless, you can notice all of these subsections will consist of great food photography and proper food and menu descriptions.  

In some short key points, you can appeal to your audience’s taste buds.

If you are copywriting for restaurants, you should definitely share how the restaurant came to be in short.

The reason behind its naming, why the place was chosen, and how the lighting, decoration, and ambiance fit the place are all things to consider. 

If your place is a café, coffee shop, or a street-side restaurant, the answer to how you should do your food copywriting will differ accordingly.

And if you are writing for a coffee shop, you should look at a few coffee copywriting examples.

Coffee is associated with relaxation, calm and quiet. So your food copywriting should be appropriate with the ambiance.

If your operation is a street-side hot vendor, it is possible that customers are looking for a quick, hot, fresh, and tasty meal from you.

In that case, your copywriting can focus on words like “hot”, “fresh”, “spicy”, “juicy”, “mouth-watering”, and stuff like that.

So based on all the food content writing examples, you can understand how the copywriting changes with your restaurant type and food type.

Now let us look at some copywriting examples for food.

 

7. Copywriting examples for food

 

In the case of food items, you should definitely appeal to the customers’ three core senses of appetite.

Of course, visual comes first when you are watching the food for the first time, whether face to face, or through menu images.

However, in written format, taste comes first. Then comes smell.

Afterward, the looks or decorations of a meal make it that much more delicious.

These three core senses are a must to touch upon in any kind of food copywriting.

For example, you can simply look at KFC’s food copywriting.

At the end of all their ads, they have their slogan “It’s finger-lickin’ good”, which directly works towards appealing to the taste buds of their customers.

It is a great example of food copywriting as well as food brand copywriting.

In addition, you can look at how Kellogg’s promotes their Special K Breakfast Shake.

The focus of the ad is how certain ingredients of food or a drink can help make you feel good. 

They advertise by mentioning that their shake contains the essence of lemons, which is full of antioxidants.

This can leave a refreshing tone to an audience.

Apart from that, you can appeal to the sense of touch or satisfying sound of bite to your target audience.

Whether it is about how smooth your burger’s bun is, or how good a munch, crunch, or crisp sound your food creates, it is sure to leave an impression.

Of course, keep in mind to showcase some amazing food photography for your brand or restaurant.

 

According to Kissmetrics, Facebook posts with photos earn 53% more likes, 104% more comments, and 84% more click-throughs.

 

Examples of fresh food through well-shot, high-quality images and well-written, creative, and fresh copywriting can definitely take your food copywriting to a whole new level.

Let us look at some more amazing copywriting examples for your food website and social media.

8. Copywriting Examples for Website

 

Food websites really can use as little reading as possible so that there is less room for delay for a consumer and their dinner.

So, food websites need a good interface, minimal, but strong and powerful keywords, and direct links connecting all of their pages.

To ensure credibility, it is recommended to have some great about us page content samples for the food website.

It simply means when you check the about us page for established quality food websites, you will find out they have enriched content with both graphics and copywriting.

Also, as we have already mentioned about keyphrases, have more research on them.

It will give you ideas about what is most looked for and searched for in search engines.

As a result, your website’s ranking will be up to the mark as your copywriting content will be SEO optimized.

The color scheme of the website, the UI, the photos used, and the text emphasized, all will play a great role to improve a food website’s user experience.

However, never forget to highlight the range of your services neatly in your about us page content.

As a result, your website’s copywriting will surely catch your consumer’s eyes and memory.

 

9. Copywriting Examples for Social Media

 

A massive portion of the market is derived from social media publicity nowadays. 

Whether you have capitalized on a trendy topic or made some clever wordplay through your copywriting, the foodies sure create a buzz around it.

The practice of posting well-crafted food and beverage photos with clever or light-hearted and witty wordplay goes well with social media audiences.

So it is a great example to capitalize on if you are a food and beverage copywriter.

Now you can ask, what other types of content can I have for my website or social media?

Let us talk about brand storytelling with that in mind.

 

10. Brand storytelling

 

Another powerful form of content writing is telling your brand’s story.

For example, Peppersmith chewing gum brand has a neat comic on their website which demonstrates how their product is made from conception to execution.

This makes them stand out from other food brands of their kind in a big way.

 

11. Food Storytelling

 

Making the story behind your food appealing is that much important as making it appetizing.

So never forget to tell how the recipe of your food item came to be.

Does the ingredient come from an unfamiliar place?

Is there a family lineage behind it?

Even if the food is common, does the tradition come from long ago?

All of this info can be powerful and strong selling points. 

Serving these pieces of information in small bits will make your food, restaurant & website that much more valuable to your potential customers. 

So never underestimate story and presentation for a powerful presence and longevity.

 

12. Keep up-to-date with new trends, techniques, and recipes

 

All great writings are inspired by many places.

So if you want to be a great food copywriter, make sure you know what is happening around you.

Whether it is your neighborhood, locality, nation, or international, trendy topics can give you an endless stream of content you can capitalize on for your food content writing or copywriting.

 

Wrapping Up: Best Examples of Great Food Copywriting

 

With all the aforementioned copywriting writing examples, you must have a better idea now about how food copywriting can be done better.

A quick reminder about what you have learned from the copy write examples mentioned before, you must be creative, intuitive, world-weary, and appealing to the five senses.

Make your food copywriting conversational.

Ask for your consumer’s opinions through your food writing.

Through comments or shares, they will let you know online.

Be light-hearted and humorous with your creative content.

It will garner more reactions and shares which will be effective marketing through your food copywriting.

Use wordplays and alliterations where you can. Those are always fun.

Moreover, use numbers in your writing effectively.

Numbers can grab attention, strengthen your copy, and drive your point across more impactfully and immediately.

In addition, do not forget about the keywords. Use long-tail descriptive keywords to appeal to your consumer’s needs and stay ahead of search engines.

 All these are the core and best examples of great food copywriting.

It is important to have a continuous stream of content ideas for food copywriter.

Hold on to these as these are observed and needed in nearly all written food advertisement examples.
